speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to be here this morning on behalf of the Minister of Transport.
I do not know why I in particular was asked to speak on behalf of the Minister of Transport. Possibly it is because he and I have certain physical features in common. I do not know but it is a great pleasure for me.
In beginning this debate on behalf of the government I would like to extend the minister's thanks to our colleagues on all sides of the House for the co-operation they have provided in making it possible for this somewhat unusual debate in which two bills are on the floor at the same time, Bill C-83 and Bill C-97.1 know that the minister wished me to extend his appreciation to the opposition. I will be very careful to ensure that the water remains here today and does not fly around the room as it did the last time I rose in this Chamber.
We are here today to debate two bills at second reading. The two bills are somewhat interconnected, in that they deal with the establishment of clear rules for conduct of business for certain aspects of marine commerce dealing with liability and insurance. I would like to make a few comments on both bills, but I will take them one at a time.
First, I will deal with the Carriage of Goods by Water Act, Bill C-83. The purpose of Bill C-83, an act respecting the transportation of goods by water, is to modernize Canadian legislation concerned with the rules of liability and compensation for damage or loss of goods during carriage by water.
The primary goal of the Hague rules is to establish uniform conditions under which shipowners or carriers are liable for loss or damage to cargo in their care. The rules set specific provisions on this liability and establish an upper limit on any claim made by cargo owners or shippers.
The new act has been the subject of much dialogue. It will adopt amendments to the original basis of the bill, the Hague rules, by increasing the shipowners' limit of liability and replacing the gold standard with the International Monetary Fund's modem currency unit, the special drawing right.

March 19, 1993
Government Orders
These amendments, known as the Hague/Visby rules, increase the limit of liability from $500 to about $1,000 per package and introduce an alternative limit of about $3 per kilo, whichever is higher. Another important amendment establishes specific provisions on liability for containerized cargo.
The development of international law in this area did not stop with the 1968 Hague/Visby rules. In 1978 a new United Nations Convention on Carriage of Goods by Sea, known as the Hamburg rules, introduced further changes to the limits of liability, burden of proof and procedures for claims.
The modifications introduced in the Hamburg rules would increase the limits of liability by about 25 per cent and would abolish the formal list of defence in support of a provision that holds the carrier liable for any loss or damage unless it is proven the carrier followed all reasonable steps to avert the loss or damage.
Generally the Hamburg rules are seen as being more favourable to shippers than the preceding international regimes. I have to mention that our industry was not unanimously in favour of adopting the Hamburg rules. Shipowners and their insurers, as well as cargo insurers and the legal community support the implementation of the Hague/Visby rules. The shippers, on the other hand, much prefer the adoption of the Hamburg rules.
Canada is not alone in not yet having adopted the newest regime. To date, the Hamburg rules have been actually adopted by only some of our trading partners, representing only about 2 per cent of our present water-borne trade.
In the absence of a consensus by our industry, a compromise approach is proposed in Bill C-83 by incorporating the Hamburg rules in schedule II. The bill requires the Minister of Transport to conduct a review and report to Parliament within six years of the adoption of the Hague/Visby rules as to whether or not they should be replaced by the Hamburg rules.
This approach will allow Canada to implement new liability rules on a gradual basis, in step with acceptance and adoption of international conventions by our trading partners. It will also demonstrate Canada's intention to accept the Hamburg rules when it is proven that they will provide a viable basis for new cargo liability conditions for international trade.
In the intervening period Canada will pursue with our trading partners the possibility of a co-ordinated action that we hope will lead to wider acceptance of the Hamburg rules in international water-borne trade.
We are in a position today to replace a badly outdated liability regime with legislation that not only brings us up to date but also positions us well for the future.
I would like to turn briefly to the second piece of legislation before us, namely Bill C-97, an act respecting marine insurance.
At the present time there is actually no federal legislation that governs the contract of marine insurance. The 1992 federal Insurance Act is confined to laws governing the operations of insurance companies while the provinces have enacted laws governing the contract of insurance, including laws over marine insurance contracts.
In 1983 the Supreme Court of Canada had to review the issue of provincial and federal jurisdiction in marine insurance. In its judgment in the Triglav case, the Supreme Court recognized that marine insurance is an integral part of maritime law and that the contract of marine insurance was a maritime contract clearly within the jurisdiction of Parliament as part of navigation and shipping.
We have been advised by our legal experts that the provincial marine insurance act may, at least in part, be inoperative as a result of this judgment by the Supreme Court.
This case brought into question the applicable law to contracts of marine insurance. It has led all interested industry groups to a unanimous position urging the government to enact a federal marine insurance act and thereby resolve the uncertainty which now exists as to the scope and application of the provincial marine insurance acts.
Bill C-97 provides a positive response to the concerns of the marine insurance industry. The proposed legislation, like the existing provincial legislation, is based on the British Marine Insurance Act of 1906 at the urging of our industry. Despite what may seem to be its extreme age, the British act is actually the most developed and widely recognized law on marine insurance. It has served as a model for national legislation in many countries.
March 19, 1993

The proposed act establishes a statutory framework for the contractual relationship of the principal parties to a contract of marine insurance, namely the insurer and the insured and their respective rights and obligations arising under the contract and the principles of indemnity for losses covered by the contract.
Not proceeding with the proposed legislation would perpetuate the current situation marked by anomalies and uncertainty that may make the conduct of marine insurance in Canada unpredictable.
I have been advised that all sectors of our marine insurance industry have strongly expressed their desire that we spare no effort in adopting the proposed legislation to correct the present situation.
Finally, in concluding my remarks on these two pieces of legislation, I would like to once again extend the thanks of the government, and in particular the Minister of Transport, to hon. colleagues on the opposite side of this Chamber for their courtesy and co-operation. The Canadian industry will be the beneficiary of the expeditious treatment of these two important bills.

Madam Speaker, we will certainly take thanks whenever we can get it from the minister.
I suggest in response to my colleague from South Shore that the reason he was asked to speak on these bills has nothing to do with his shape at all. Rather it is not only the fact of his proclivity for spreading water around the Chamber when he speaks, but also the fact that as a maritimer, he is clearly learned in the intricacies of these two bills. That was a very concise and erudite explanation of a complex area of law. He is to be congratulated for it.
Really, there is not a great deal to add on these topics except to say I find the areas interesting as legal matters. We rarely deal with matters that might be described as private law in this Chamber. Most of the legislation we enact here is of a more broad public policy nature and the areas of private law normally fall to provincial jurisdiction.
This is an exception as a result of the fact that in C-83 we have the implementation of an international convention and in C-97, as a result of a Supreme Court of
Government Orders
Canada decision, we are dealing with insurance law which would normally be in the provincial jurisdiction. However, because in this case it relates to matters of international maritime commerce, the court has found that federal jurisdiction is touched upon as well. Therefore C-97 in that case attempts to create an interlocking relationship of federal and provincial law that ensures that maritime insurance is covered by a statutory framework.
There have been a number of submissions made to the minister as well as to the opposition parties concerning these bills. An example that I brought with me this morning from The Canadian Board of Marine Underwriters, referring to both bills, says:
Both bills are very important to the Canadian maritime industry, and will help to ensure the efficiency and competitiveness of Canadian importers, exporters and marine insurers alike. For that reason, all sectors of the maritime industry have supported the legislation.
It is of some concern to us that since an election must be held in 1993, either or both bills might not receive passage in time to be enacted. We would therefore urge you to do your utmost to see that both bills receive priority attention in order that they may become law.
I know we all eagerly hope there will be an election in 1993 and so we share the concern of the industry that these bills be dealt with in an expeditious manner. I did hear this morning that perhaps the Minister of National Defence will be looking for a way to suspend the Constitution in order to avoid having an election this year. However, we will put that in the category of rumour and carry on with the assumption that we will be going to the polls this year.
In that case, the reference of these bills to the Standing Committee on Transport creates quite an extensive work-load for the transport committee. The minister just last week referred the report of the National Transportation Act Review Commission to that committee as well and asked us to report on that by the end of June.
I would suggest, particularly in light of the disagreement among sectors of the industry on Bill C-83 as to what set of rules ought to apply, that the committee will need to review many of the implications of Bill C-83 and hear witnesses from the industry on that matter.

March 19, 1993
Government Orders
For our part, I would like to say we will do everything we can to try to expedite those hearings so that the bill can be properly considered and brought back to the House as the first priority. Perhaps this will be prior to entering into the detailed consideration of the review commission report, which as I say is also before the committee.
In juggling these priorities I would like to say that from our point of view, and I will be interested to hear what the NDP has to say about it, these bills should come first. They do require hearings. They do require witnesses, particularly on Bill C-83. We will attempt to have them back to the House as quickly as possible.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to the two bills, Bill C-83, an act respecting the transportation of goods by water, and Bill C-97, an act respecting marine insurance.
I indicate right at the outset that we support these two measures, which basically are bringing marine law and marine insurance law into the 1990s. We will do whatever we can to quickly proceed through committee.
In fact, one of the reasons we want the bills to go to transport committee is that there are people on that committee who have a sense of the maritime industry already. They are well positioned to know what is in these bills and to determine what aspects of them need to be looked at and then move them back to the House. I honestly do not expect much of a delay there.
In terms of the transportation of goods by water the government speaker took us on a European tour with respect to The Hague Visby rules and the Hamburg rules. The bill is designed to allow the Minister of Transport to bring those rules forward when the marine industry of Canada decides it is time.
If we look at the breakdown in terms of the value of Canadian water-borne trade, we will see that almost 60 per cent of our commerce moves under The Hague Visby rules, $11 billion or 19 per cent under The Hague rules and only 2 per cent under the Hamburg rules. So we have a long way to go in terms of matching what the industry is doing.
I have one suggestion which I intend to have raised in committee. Under Bill C-83 there is a provision which says that: "The Minister of Transport shall within six years after the coming into force of Part I"-which is The Hague Visby rules- "(a) consider whether The Hague Visby rules should be replaced by the Hamburg rules; and (b) cause a report setting out the results of that consideration to lay before the House of Parliament".
There are two points. The minister can do that at any time during those six years. I think it needs to be clear in the act that the six years run out on December 31, 1999.
In addition, we have just gone through one process mandated by law that required a formal review of the National Transportation Act. There were hundreds of thousands, if not millions of dollars spent to review that act and the report was tabled last week.
The Transportation Safety Board had the same kind of mechanism built into it but only after three years of the act being in place. Now we are embarked on the same kind of course. In effect they have set up a commission which will spend taxpayers' money to review an act that is only three years old. By the very testimony of the chairman of the board the act is working quite well, thank you very much.
What I am suggesting is that in addition to what is in this bill the matter should automatically be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport at that time. Whenever the minister decides it is time to evaluate whether or not we move from the Hague Visby rules to the Hamburg rules, he would table it in Parliament and it would then be automatically referred to the Standing Committee on Transport. It will review it and send back a recommendation to the House as to whether or not we should move forward with whatever the minister's recommendation may be.
He or she may decide it is still not time to move forward to the Hamburg rules. We could call witnesses from the industry and get a sense from them and then we could report back to Parliament with our own recommendation that may or may not be consistent with the minister's. What it does is save taxpayers money, quite frankly. It saves having to go outside for a commission. It
March 19, 1993

allows some protection for Parliament from a minister just going ahead and changing the rules, so to speak.
I think the committee should look at that as a possible change in approach as to how we deal with this legislation. In any event, that is Bill C-83, the transportation of goods by water.
In terms of the marine insurance, clearly we are updating Canadian law because of a court case that brought into question whether or not Canadian law applied as opposed to provincial law. I am sure that once the officials come before us at committee we will get some sense of the nuts and bolts of that. I will be honest I am not familiar with the intricacies of insurance, let alone marine insurance.
There are some interesting clauses in this bill. I just want to read them into the record because I think they will pique some people's interest in terms of the weirdness in some ways of legalese.
For example, clause 18 states: "Every contract by way of gaming or wagering is void". Does this mean that people sort of gamble away their ships? Is that what this means and therefore there is some protection there? That might be a question worth raising with the officials. Schedule III, construction of marine policies, has some interesting wording too.
We have had some experiences in this House with marine legislation where we were trying to bring it into the modern era, the modern language, eliminating flogging for example on board vessels which was in the Canada Shipping Act until about 1986 or 1987. We finally got rid of that antiquated method of keeping the seafarers in line.
Things do move slowly.

Things do move slowly, yes. Actually a lot of these bills that we are dealing with today are based on a 1924 law passed by Great Britain. We are just sort of fine-tuning it. It takes time in the House of Commons and the bowels of the bureaucracy to have these things worked through.
In fact, on Bill C-83 there was a white paper, a discussion paper in 1984 that led to the bill today. It took eight years, from 1984 to 1992, not for a philosophical bill, but for a nuts and bolts bill to work its way through the consultation which has to happen, the justice department in terms of legalese and what have you.
Government Orders
Back to some of the more interesting clauses in this schedule:
"pirates" includes passengers on the insured ship who mutiny and persons who attack the ship from land;
That is interesting but what happens if it is a pirate from another ship? Is that covered elsewhere in the bill? It is an interesting matter to raise.
Another clause in the schedule states:
"thieves" does not include persons who commit a clandestine theft or passengers, officers or members of the crew of the injured ship who commit a theft.
I am not quite sure I understand that kind of wording.
Here is an interesting one: In a marine policy a reference (b) to arrests, "and of kings, princes and people includes political or executive acts, but does not include riot or ordinary judicial process". Kings, princes and people, that is interesting.
Indeed, perils of the seas means fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas but does not include ordinary action of the wind and waves.
Over the last while, we have seen the reality of the normal action of wind and waves with two major casualties, one on our coast and one on the coast of Great Britain. In a serious way, we need to take a look at the ramifications of that particular clause.
For those people who really find that legalese drives them crazy, here is the classic. This is under number (2) in a marine policy, reference (c): "To average unless general means a partial loss of the subject matter insured other than a general average loss but does not include particularly charges". Perhaps the government speaker might want to explain to the House what that particular clause means.
As I said at the outset, we support the two pieces of legislation. We agreed that they should be combined for the purpose of debate. We want the bills to go the transport committee because it will be in a position to give them speedier consideration.
I do not think we should wait another 10 years for these bills to come back. We should pass them at second reading now, get them into committee, back out of committee, given third reading and then on to the other place as quickly as we can. It helps the maritime industry do its job in an efficient and in a less expensive way.

March 19, 1993

Madam Speaker, I have a message here from the Greek community of my riding.
The Skopje regime insists on seeking international recognition of its multi-ethnic former Yugoslav republic under the name of Macedonia, while leaders of the various ethnic groups accuse this regime of ignoring the wishes of the majority of the population on the issue of the republic's name and of violations of their basic human rights.
I would like our government to inform our Parliament whether these accusations are being taken into account, considering that ethnic Albanians alone constitute more than one-third of the total population.

Madam Speaker, no nation in today's highly competitive world market will be able to bring about economic renewal without first having a well-trained and adaptable work force.
Such a work force comes about only when labour and management work together. Our ability to generate wealth and be successful in the global economy will depend on that.
The best way to build a highly skilled and highly relative work force is through a revised national apprenticeship program.
Canada's apprenticeship program has fallen into great disrepute. No longer is it seen as an integral part of our education system, but rather it is looked upon as a dead end by prospective students.
March 19, 1993

When is the government going to show some understanding and appreciation of the nation's lack of skilled tradesmen? When is the government going to announce a renewed, revitalized national apprenticeship program that will address the pressing current need in Canada for a well-trained work force? Canada can no longer afford a hit and miss approach to apprenticeship programs.

Madam Speaker, on January 23, 1992 the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that Alberta requires a licence under the Navigable Waters Protection Act for the Oldman River dam. The Supreme Court upheld the March 13, 1990 Federal Court of Appeal ruling which quashed the required licence and ordered an environmental assessment and review of the dam.
The number one recommendation of the EARP report was to decommission the dam. The federal Ministers of Environment and Transport proved to be too wimpy to accept the fact that the dam is both environmentally and economically unsound. They rejected the number one recommendation but promised to implement the other 22.
On May 2, 1992 the Minister of Transport said of the 22 recommendations: "We will ensure that they are implemented". By November 19, 1992 not one recommendation had been implemented and the minister lamely promised: "We are going to see that these 22 recommendations are implemented".
Spring run-off is about to begin and the negative impacts will take effect.
Canadians should take note that the Conservatives refuse to obey the Supreme Court of Canada or stand up for their own promises. These ministers are the fat, wingless ducks of the Oldman River.

Madam Speaker, one way that my community is trying to regain economic activity and diversify its economy is by helping local people prepare to start their own businesses.
The Brock University Centre for Entrepreneurship, Niagara College and the innovative New Enterprise Store are teaching potential entrepreneurs the techniques necessary to establish their own businesses. The Niagara Enterprise Agency is also being established to help identify potential entrepreneurs in the plants that are closing and provide them with the training necessary to commence their own businesses.
Training programs are also in place to help train people for the opportunities that will be created by these new businesses.
However, local entrepreneurs are all too often running into the same problem. This is an inability to obtain the necessary capital to put their ideas into effect. Many of these new businesses do not have the assets which they can mortgage in order to obtain the needed financing. Government programs like the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Small Business Financing Program and the Federal Business Development Bank make financing available, but we must do more.

Madam Speaker, November 21 is the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.
Racism, anti-Semitism and racial discrimination are among the most destructive forces within any society. Our Charter of Rights and Freedoms prohibits discrimination based on religion, colour or place of origin. However, the charter cannot solve all of our societal problems.
To solve the social problem of racial and anti-Semitic discrimination and crime is to address the education system. School curricula at all levels must ensure that a component is taught in the classroom on the issue of race relations. From the very earliest stages through post-secondary education our school system must reflect our cultural mosaic.

March 19, 1993
I call on the government to establish a national depository of racial and anti-Semitic crimes in our society. Through such a depository, proper planning can be done to establish programs to respond to the challenges of racial harmony. We must act now to ensure that Canadians of all backgrounds continue to live and work in the finest nation on earth.

Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity today to congratulate the Third Holland Landing Guide Troop for taking a interest in the future of this country as it relates to the problems of pollution in Lake Simcoe.
These young ladies have learned that fishing and tourism are veiy important to the people of Georgina. They also understand that Lake Simcoe is in big trouble and these guides think pollution is "very wrong", to quote them directly.
They are concerned that if the province of Ontario puts a giant mega-dump within one mile of Lake Simcoe it will affect the spawning ground, which is very near the proposed dump site. This has the potential of making the pollution in Lake Simcoe that much worse.
These young guides do not want to get anywhere near or go swimming anywhere near a dump. They feel Lake Simcoe has enough problems already because of fertilizers, sewage and other pollution. The quality of the water is already at risk in Lake Simcoe. They recognize that most of the fish which are caught in Lake Simcoe have been put there as a result of being raised in a fish hatchery because the algae and the pollutants that are now in the lake have ruined many of the spawning areas-

Painful cuts were necessary and they were made, but they were tempered with compassion. This was not the situation in the provinces of Manitoba or Newfoundland, which also made budget announcements this week.
The slash and burn policies implemented by the Conservatives in Manitoba called for devastating cuts to 56 social service industries which are the front-line advocates for the poor and disenfranchised, those most affected by failed PC economic policies.
The Liberals in Newfoundland also decided that hiring investigators to crack down on social assistance abuse, cutting grants to volunteer organizations and cutting Public Service jobs without notice is their solution. Madam Speaker, Saskatchewan has some world-class companies underpinned by world-class technology.
I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate one of those companies, Flexi-Coil Ltd. of Saskatoon. People from Regina do not often congratulate people in Saskatoon, but this is one of those strange times.
March 19, 1993

Flexi-Coil manufactures farm machinery and its order books are overflowing. In fact, employment at the company has just doubled in seven months from 430 to more than 800 right now.
What is driving the company's success? The answer is research and development and leading-edge technology that allows seeding operations in high moisture conditions with minimal soil disturbance.
Flexi-Coil has not bought the argument that Saskatchewan is too far from major markets. Instead, it is developing international markets and putting people to work.

Madam Speaker, the Minister for Science and the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, in responding yesterday to a question, said that we have a surplus of trade with foreign countries of $9.5 billion.
I would like to remind the minister that trade includes goods, services and financial flows, and those numbers are disastrous. The current account deficit with foreign countries amounts to $30 billion lor 1992.1 wonder when the minister is going to come clean with the Canadian public and portray the real economic situation of the country. For example, we have a national debt of $650 billion, which amounts to 95 per cent of the gross domestic product, equivalent to Brazil and Venezuela.

Madam Speaker, oil and gas has faced a bad economic environment almost continuously since late 1985. Among western Canadians alone employment is down by about
35,000	jobs over the past eight years, partly because of our high dollar.
Even with gradual price recovery the number of jobs is still expected to decline by about 18 per cent by 1995. To put that in more human terms, another 11,700 families in western Canada will face the prospect of job losses.
We need to restore profitability and competitiveness to our domestic energy industry if it is to be rejuvenated.
The federal government has a role to play in the revitalization of the sector, which provides close to
100,000	direct jobs in Alberta alone. According to one estimate, 30,000 new jobs would be created in the west and throughout the Canadian economy for every billion dollars in new investment in our oil and gas industry.
With no change in the fiscal regime, industry investment this year might drop to $4.1 billion, or 85 per cent of forecast cash flow. The federal government has shown a commitment, thank goodness, to oil and gas in the Atlantic provinces. It could also stimulate the oil patch in the west.

Madam Speaker, passengers using Vancouver International Airport will soon be paying a special tax of $5 to $15. This tax will be imposed on travellers by the Vancouver International Airport Authority in order to fund its capital construction plans.
This is a tax that could not come at a worse time for Canada's airline industry, but the villain here is not the local airport authority. Instead, New Democrats hold the Minister of Transport responsible.
We in this party warned Canadians that there would be hidden costs to the transfer of control of airports to local authorities. Sadly, we have once again been proven correct.
Successive Conservative transport ministers have imposed deregulation, reducing the government's role and responsibility in transport matters.
Canada is now reaping the bitter fruits of Tory free market philosophy with catastrophe in all transport modes. Now there is one more burden for the Canadian consumer: another tax on travel thanks to Tory transport policy. Regretfully it is one more reason for traffic to divert from Vancouver to Seattle in Bellingham, Washington.

Canadian municipalities are still trying to obtain a reversal of the 1992 freeze imposed by the government on the portion of municipal taxes applied to federal property.

All finance ministers, no matter what their political stripe, including Newfoundland's minister of finance to give him full credit, agreed that deficit reduction was the number one priority in this country. He said: Madam Speaker, I would like to speak to the amendments I have put forward and begin by thanking my hon. friends opposite for their co-operation, particularly those in the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party who participated in the legislative committee on Bill C-113, in allowing these amendments to come before the House. I would like to apologize and thank Your Honour and the Ihble for the difficult procedural challenge I presented with these amendments as they have come forward.
These amendments are extremely important to the manufacturing sector in Atlantic Canada and members of the Atlantic Transportation Commission who first brought forward their necessity to the legislative committee on Bill C-113 and indeed the government.
The reduction in subsidies introduced in the December economic statement of the Minister of Finance would have cut the subsidies provided under the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act by 10 per cent.
Shortly thereafter the Atlantic Transportation Commission on behalf of manufacturers in Atlantic Canada approached the government. As business people they respected and appreciated the government's deficit control efforts and wished to support the government in its deficit control efforts. Their request was that instead of an across the board reduction in the subsidies they would prefer a selective application of the subsidies that would be more in tune with the concept for which these statutes were initiated in the first place.
I might remind the House briefly that these programs came about going back to the Duncan commission on maritime claims in 1926, after which the Maritime Freight Rates Act was brought in. Those statutes respond to the National Transportation Act in its intention and recognition of transportation as a key to regional economic development and commercial viability.
In Atlantic Canada manufacturers and producers are in effect price takers rather than price setters in the marketplace. As such they must generally absorb all or a major part of outbound transportation, particularly when selling into central and western Canada.
The Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act provide a reduction in freight rates for the movement of commodities that have been manufactured or produced in Atlantic Canada. That in effect makes it more possible for Atlantic Canadian manufacturers to be competitive in the larger markets of central Canada.
What has been brought forward in the proposals encapsulated in this set of amendments would see, rather than 10 per cent across the board, no change in the basic subsidy for the selective westbound; in the basic westbound, a 5 per cent reduction and in the inter-regional, a 10 per cent reduction. Household goods would be eliminated from the basic westbound. Scrap and waste materials would be eliminated from the basic westbound. At the same time during the first year of the program there would be data collected with a view to making further modifications next year.
It is important to say that members of the House, in having amendments before them for discussion, are hearing what has been said to government, indeed to all parties, by Atlantic businessmen and manufacturers. It is going to be beneficial. It brings those two statutes back to their original purposes in terms of supporting manufacturing enterprises. I am sure it will be very well greeted by the business community in Atlantic Canada and the people whose jobs depend on those manufacturing enterprises.
I thank the House and strongly recommend the support of these amendments by all members.

Let us not fool ourselves. This is not just an exercise in deficit reduction. This is not just an exercise of down loading to the provinces or the municipalities. When it comes to the section of the Western Grain Transportation Act we are down loading into the pockets of the farmers. This is not a reduction in the rates charged by the railways. This is a reduction in the amount of money used to offset the cost to the producer.
Whether it is $1, $2, or $3 a tonne, that money has to come out of the pockets of farmers who have already been bled dry because of the price of grain around the world, thanks to the Americans and the Europeans in terms of the subsidy war. It costs a lot of farmers more to produce grain than what they get when they sell it. The government has decided to put more onus on those farmers to pick up the cost.
I am wondering what all this is about. It has to do with a law that was passed on September 28, 1988. It is called Public Law 100-449, entitled U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. I want to quote from an interesting section of it. It is section 304 that deals with negotiations regarding certain sectors' biannual reports. Referring to the President of the United States it says: "(a) in general and (2) as an exercise of the foreign relations powers of the President under the Constitution, the President will enter into immediate consultations with the Government of Canada to obtain the exclusion from the transportation rates established under Canada's Western Grain Transportation Act of agricultural goods that originate in Canada and are shipped by east coast ports for consumption in the United States".
How much of the free trade agreement agenda is found in Bill C-113? Certainly my colleagues will argue
Government Orders
that the whole question of the cuts to UI does nothing more than parallel what is available in a number of our competitor States today.
Obviously the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission has been successful in convincing the government that there is a better way to make these cuts. I give it credit for coming forward and taking a look at some of the elements in the current legislation that perhaps skew things in Atlantic Canada.
For example, the provision that scrap metal can be subsidized means that it is cheaper to send scrap metal to Hamilton or Sault Ste. Marie than it is for the metal to go to Sysco in Cape Breton. That does not make sense.
The subsidy for household goods is used primarily by federal employees who are being reimbursed by the government in any case to move their household goods from Atlantic Canada when they are transferred back across the country, whether it is DND, the RCMP or whatever.
Those things make sense. I understand why the APTC put them forward to get a reduction and more power to the commission, but I want to ask the government where the same consideration was for federal public servants who were told that they were having their wages restricted as a means of helping the government's deficit plan. Did the government sit down with them and work out a way in which perhaps money could be saved? There was not one discussion.
What about the unemployed who are being hammered by this bill? The unemployed who for whatever reason have to quit a job without having another one to go to are to be denied UI benefits entirely. Did this government sit down with those people and say: "Is there a better way?" Did it even ask: "If we put you back to work, will that help the deficit?" Of course it will. Those are areas my colleagues will pursue as they participate in this debate.
I want to return to the Western Grain Transportation Act. If the government was legitimately concerned about the act and the manner in which the funding is offered, it would recognize, as the Standing Committee on Transport did, that there are some imbalances in the act. It does not treat both directions in the same way. It does not provide assistance to the marine sector to take the

March 19, 1993
Government Orders
grain that comes to the port of Thunder Bay and move it to an export position in the St. Lawrence River.
The transport committee has recommended that on an interim basis the marine component be covered. That will stimulate the economy in eastern Canada because right now we are in danger of not having enough ships to move the crops from western Canada. The reality is that the west coast is plugged. One more bushel of grain cannot be moved through Prince Rupert or Vancouver. None of us want grain being moved through Seattle because we want the jobs to stay in Canada. If we do not act and provide for a better balance we are not going to have enough ships on the Great Lakes. We are not going to have enough people left in Thunder Bay to handle the grain, clean it, weigh it and trans-ship it. As a nation we are in danger of losing our ability to be flexible. The same arguments can be made for Churchill as well.
What the government is doing now by cutting the Western Grain Transportation Act is saying to the seaway: "No, we are not going to give you any more money. We are not going to help you out. We are going to let you go down the tubes". At the same time it is saying to the farmers: "We lied to you years ago when we passed this act".
The Liberals passed the Western Grain Transportation Act, and the Tories have not bothered to deal with its inequities. They were saying at the time: "Trust us. Do not woriy, it is in the law. It cannot be changed. The formula is firm". We have just proven that it is not firm. The government arbitrarily cuts 10 per cent and attacks the farmers at the same time, both in terms of the next two or three years by making them pay more for their transportation and also by sending them a signal that the Western Grain Transportation Act is up for grabs.
Certainly the United States would like us to get rid of it. My sense is that this government would like us to get rid of it, because of this warped sense that we have to get rid of the deficit.
We do not necessarily disagree with getting rid of the deficit and bringing it down to a manageable level, but we do disagree with doing it by attacking people. That is not the way. We need to put more money in the hands of people so they can get out there and buy consumer goods, create jobs and therefore create new taxpayers.
This is true for the bill itself in its entirety, but these three clauses in particular are going to undermine the fabric of this country. We on this side, my caucus, have no choice but to propose the kind of amendments that I have put forward to eliminate the clause that reduces the Western Grain Transportation Act by 10 per cent and to eliminate the clause that reduces in any way the freight subsidy in Atlantic Canada. We need to protect those areas of subsidy because in doing so we are protecting the regions and we are protecting the people.
For the government to bring forward this kind of legislation shows quite frankly that it does not care any more. It does not care about Atlantic Canada. It does not care about the unemployed. It does not care about western Canada. It does not care about any part of this country.
Therefore I am going to continue to oppose this bill, as will my colleagues. I am pleased that the member for Regina-Lumsden was able to second my motion, because of anybody in this House he is not only the most knowledgeable member on transportation but the strongest defender of the prairie farmers and the most vociferous opponent of the kind of cuts that we are seeing here today.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Madam Speaker, I am happy that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission was able to talk a little sense into the government as this bill was passing through the committee and achieve the modest relief that is represented in the amendment.
The commission is fighting a losing battle and it has been, along with other transportation groups in Atlantic Canada, for the last several years this government has been in power. In Atlantic Canada we are seeing, through other legislation, the erosion of subsidies to grain producers and grain consumers in Atlantic Canada, as well as an erosion of the transportation infrastructure generally in Atlantic Canada.
This has been the legacy of this Conservative government. It is one that has been very much on the minds of industries that use transportation services, be it to bring grain or other products in from central Canada or to send our own products such as food products, pulp and paper and our basic resources across Atlantic Canada and through the rail system and the road network out to market elsewhere in Canada and the United States.
March 19, 1993

This may be a small victory, and I would certainly respect the ability of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission to speak on behalf of transporters in Atlantic Canada. It has proven itself in other instances to be a responsible advocate of the transportation industry in Atlantic Canada. It is certainly willing to work within the confines of legislation that is put before it.
Certainly this legislation does very little to enhance the ability of our industry, producers and consumers in Atlantic Canada to receive a level playing field when it comes to east-west transportation. The amendment before us does not exonerate the bill itself, which we continue to oppose.

Madam Speaker, I have a feeling of deja vu. I have a feeling we have been here before, between 1980 and 1984 when the Liberals abolished the Crows Nest Pass freight rate agreement of 1897 and implemented the Western Grain Transportation Act over my objections and the objections of my colleagues and major farm organizations.
It got to the point where the prairie wheat pools reluctantly accepted the abolishing of that rate and the increased freight rates for grain producers. It reluctantly accepted those changes because of the guarantee of a basic rail network, the guarantee of a sufficient supply of grain cars and the guarantee that the Government of Canada would continue to pay its share of the freight rates under the Western Grain Transportation Act.
This bill proposes to reduce the government's share of the cost of moving that grain by 10 per cent, which means that the difference will have to be picked up by farmers.
Ever since 1984 the grain producers of western Canada have been paying an ever-increasing amount of the cost of moving grain. In 1986-87 their share was $5.97 a tonne. For 1991-92 it had almost doubled to $11.07 a tonne. For the current year it will be $14.12 a tonne. That is an almost threefold increase in the farmers' share of the cost of moving grain, while grain prices have been steadily dropping since the 1980-81 crop year. They have gone down almost every single year.
Government Orders
The prairie wheat pools, representing 100,000 grain producers in the three prairie provinces, made it clear that it does not like, does not accept and does not agree with this provision in the bill. It says that its concern about the expenditure cuts legislation lies in the section that deals with a 10 per cent cut to the assistance paid by the federal government under the Western Grain Transportation Act.
The WGTA was implemented in 1984 under the Liberal government and with reluctant support by the Tories, or at least they said they were reluctant. Prairie farmers reluctantly gave up fixed freight rates and accepted increasing freight costs in exchange for a guarantee of service from the railways and a commitment of a constant amount of assistance from the federal government. This assistance, the Crow benefit, was set up in perpetuity in the Western Grain Transportation Act.
The Tories have done it again. They have even brought an end to perpetuity. It was only on the condition that the prairie grain producers had this guarantee in perpetuity that they reluctantly went along with the abolishing of the Crows Nest Pass freight rates.
If this is not a betrayal, if this is not going back on the word of the Government of Canada, of the Parliament of Canada, then I do not know what is.
I want to say to the Minister of Supply and Services that he can inform his four colleagues from Saskatchewan that not a damned one of them is going to be back here. There will be no Tories from Saskatchewan, just as there are no Liberals from Saskatchewan. Both parties are going to be wiped out because of what they did from 1980 to 1984 and what they are doing again now.
We have no money to spend on it.

If the hon. member knew what a bushel of wheat looked like if it hit him in the face I would be prepared to listen to him. He can get up and make his own speech later.

March 19, 1993
Government Orders
The United States Congress is proposing to authorize the President of the United States to disallow grain moving from Canada to the United States under the Western Grain Transportation Act for United States consumption. If that is not a direct interference in the internal affairs, sovereignty and independence of Canada then I do not know what is.
The government has taken action, to its credit, to intervene and prevent the American government from making American subsidiaries obey United States' law in Canada. The government put a stop to that kind of interference. It damn well has to put a stop to this kind of interference as well.
The equalized grain rates, the subsidized grain rates, are meant to put Canadian grain producers in an even position, a level playing field-the Tories want to call everything a level playing field. What the hell is the use of having a level playing field if the other guy has the ball on our 10-yard line all the time?
The average haul for Canadian grain producers is over 900 miles, for American producers it is about 700 miles, and for producers in Australia and Argentina it is under 200 miles. In order to have equal competition with grain-exporting countries we devised a freight rate system that put our grain producers in the Canadian Wheat Board in a position in which they could compete. Now the government wants the farmers to pick up some more of the tab.
It is kicking them when they are down. I guess that is the way the Tories fight, that is the way they govern. They kick them when they are down.
We warned about this in the period from 1980 to 1984 when the Liberals were in power. We told them what would happen. They pooh-poohed us, would not believe us. Railway companies would not believe us and declared they would not be doing the things we said they would. They have done it. The railways are now applying to abandon even some of those rail lines that are guaranteed in the basic network until the year 2000. So much for their guarantees. So much for the government's guarantees. So much for the government's law that says that these are guaranteed in perpetuity.
Any benefit we were getting out of the Western Grain Transportation Act, supposedly in perpetuity, supposedly with guarantees, is being wiped out with a stroke of a pen by this government.
I do not understand why it has to do this. The impact it will have on the deficit is negligible. But the impact it will have on grain producers to the tune of about an additional $2 per tonne will be $2 per tonne less that they will spend in their communities. It will be be $2 a tonne less that they will spend on buying farm machinery which is manufactured in eastern Canada; $2 a tonne less to survive.
While thousands and thousands of our grain producers over the last several years have gone bankrupt and lost land that had been in their hands for three and four generations, the Tories, the Liberals, the press and free enterprise call it a recession.
In some respect what they are going through in western Canada right now is a depression and in some respect it is worse than what the grain farmers experienced in the dirty thirties. Tory times are tough times. Tory times and Liberal times are dirty times like the dirty thirties. It is time to put a stop to this.
We must not allow this to happen to our grain producers again. Enough is enough. I hope that hon. members will see that this has to be stopped. I hope that the Liberals will be willing to admit the errors of their ways and that they were wrong between 1980 and 1984.
Now they are opposing this kind of measure. They did not then. I hope that they will admit the errors of their ways and confess their sins of omission and commission. Vote for this amendment. I hope government members, particularly those of the three prairie provinces, will think twice before they vote for this kind of legislation.

He had a further difficulty in that he suggested that somehow the NDP provincial government in that province had changed things around. It had a budget yesterday that changed things around all right. It is a change from the Tories, I agree, but it behaved just like the federal Tories.

Madam Speaker, I am rising on the amendment. I want to say that the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden has not lost any of his fire over the years he has served in this House. It is always a treat to hear him.
I want to speak to the amendment and to the reasons this government is bringing forward the changes to the Crow rate. These reasons affect not just the prairies but also the west coast. They affect the grain workers in British Columbia. They also affect railway workers.
Last year the railway bypassed British Columbia, bypassed the Vancouver grain terminals and shipped Canadian grain to Seattle. They shipped that grain to Seattle for trans-shipment overseas on a trial basis. The trial failed. Seattle grain terminals were not clean. They were full of pesticides. They were full of rodents. The terminals were filthy.
At a port of destination, Canadian grain, which has always had a reputation for being of the highest standard in the world was found to be unacceptable and certainly not up to its normal standards. This bypassing of the grain terminals in British Columbia was abandoned. The trial did not work.
It is passing strange that this proposal to cut the Crow rate comes on the heels of this experiment. One would not want to presuppose that this government would be at all mischievous nor would one want to presuppose that this government was even so together as to be able to come at an issue from a number of fronts at the same time.

March 19, 1993
Government Orders
Here we have a trial run to bypass grain terminals in British Columbia with the railway, affecting grain and railway workers. Then we have a proposal, a piece of legislation introduced in the House to cut the Crow rate. Now the grain and railway workers in British Columbia have been advised that there are discussions going on to develop a north-south transportation route for grain. Guess where the terminals are going to be. The terminals are going to be in Mexico.
Is it not funny that this government is racing to ram through a North American free trade agreement? It is not just all the other jobs we have been talking about fleeing Canada and going to Mexico, now we are talking about Canadian grain going through Mexican terminals to other ports of entry.
This is the rumour and believe me the workers are worried. They have not been able to verify all of it but they certainly have a lot of bits of information that lead both the grain and railway workers to believe that is the intent of this government.
If this is the plan of the government not only are we facing cuts in Crow rates and other impacts on the other industries in British Columbia, we are now facing Canadian railway workers being bypassed for American railway workers and Canadian grain workers being bypassed for Mexican grain workers.
Here we will have a situation.
We have no control over the cleanliness of the terminals. We just heard today during Question Period that it is a proven fact and the Mexicans are admitting that they have no control over the environment, no control at all over how many or what kind of pesticides would be used in those terminals in Mexico.
Put all these little pieces together and you start to see a picture of deceit and collusion and funny-headed thinking about what is good for Canada.
The hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan said: "If the Government of Canada could negotiate with the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission for a better way to cut freight subsidies why, I would ask you, could it not negotiate with the Canadian public sector workers for a better way to cut costs than to freeze their wages arbitrarily as it is doing in this bill?"
Here we have a government which took the time to negotiate with the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Committee for a better way to cut freight subsidies and then arbitrarily introduced legislation to freeze public sector workers' wages. The government has a legislative responsibility to negotiate with them.
It brings in a piece of legislation and says: "Here it is, no wage increase for you folks for two years. We are off negotiating with other people; we do not have time to negotiate with you".
I would suggest that again we see in this bill on three counts this government abrogating its responsibility to Canadians: a responsibility to Canadian workers to negotiate their wages; the responsibility to the west and the jobs in the west, to negotiate Crow rate changes, not arbitrarily implement then, but negotiate them as they did with the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission.
The third is to arbitrarily kick the heck out of unemployed workers in this country who have no control over what the government has done to this economy.
I very much appreciate the opportunity to put these issues before the people of Canada and I hope the government will rethink this bill, particularly as it comes to the Crow rate prior to this bill being put to a vote.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part in this debate. It is possible that we should actually consider debate on this amendment today to be the Les Benjamin memorial debate because for those of us who were not part of the House of Commons before 1984, there is a legend which exists.
That is the legend of the great Crow debate, the legend which led to New Democrat members from every conceivable constituency across Canada standing up to speak out in favour of the Crow benefit for western farmers.
I will tell you that the legend lives in our caucus. There are people who have never seen a field of wheat, who have never been to Saskatchewan, who made passionate speeches during that debate. They made passionate speeches because of the leadership which the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden gave to our caucus at that stage.

This is the last term which that member will be here as part of our caucus, unfortunately.
I want, as I start my comments on this, to pay tribute to his contribution over the years to the New Democratic Party. I also want to tell people across this country that debate and that fight took place at a time when the New Democratic Party was down in the polls. In fact, it took place at at time when we were much lower in the polls than we presently are. It was one of the key ingredients that demonstrated yet again to the people of Canada that there is one party that will stand up for average Canadians. There is one party which will fight on behalf of people who are not privileged, who are not rich, people who have been picked on and betrayed throughout their history. That has been the New Democratic Party. That will continue to be the New Democratic Party.
The fight that the member for Regina-Lumsden led back in 1984 and which has passed into the history and traditions of our caucus will be something which will continually be a source of inspiration to all of us who are part of this caucus.
Some members in the Liberal Party say this is an example of the New Democratic Party defending the status quo. Let me suggest it is an example of the New Democratic Party defending solemn promises made to the people of this country. I know that is something that neither the Conservatives nor the Liberals understand, the notion of a solemn promise made by a government to the people.
The Liberal Party made a solemn promise to the people in western Canada that the Crow rate would exist forever. It is not surprising because it was a return for tremendous benefits, tremendous handouts given to the Canadian Pacific Railway. This was a tremendous giveaway in terms of tax, in terms of land, in terms of privileges of every sort. In return for that the Crow benefit was to be maintained in place forever, a sacred promise which the Liberals broke.
It was a sacred promise which they broke when they brought in the Western Grain Transportation Act, the WGTA. That too, though it broke a sacred promise,
Government Orders
offered a new sacred promise, that there would be benefits paid to the railways to keep the rates for grain transportation down in the future for all western grain transported in perpetuity. It was a sacred promise.
The Liberals broke one sacred promise but offered another. The Conservatives raged against that broken promise of the Liberals in 1984. I hope I am not mistaken. I suspect they stood up beside the member for Regina-Lumsden and said: "It is terrible that the Conservatives have to stand up for these promises that the Liberal Party is so abjectly breaking". Today we have this same Conservative Party breaking that further sacred promise and making things even worse for the people who produce and sell grain from western Canada.
How much of this damage is going to be inflicted on western farmers? The estimated reduction in transportation subsidies is estimated at $73 million for 1993-94; $104 million in 1994-95.
The retiring president of the National Parmers' Union has estimated that for western farmers it means an increase in transportation costs and therefore a reduction in the amount of money which they will receive for their grain of from $2 to $2.50 per tonne. That is a major bite at a time when all of us in the House of Commons know that western farmers are being hammered. They are being hit as never before, with the possible exception of the 1930s.
In the 1930s it could be put down to problems with weather, at least in part. What is hitting farmers in western Canada now is damage which is inflicted by the policies of the United States with respect to the massive subsidies for grain exports which it has put into place.
Once again in the House of Commons there is just one party standing up and saying that the broken promises of the Liberals in 1984 deserve to be remembered and the broken promises of the Conservatives in 1993 deserve to be remembered.
We are talking about a betrayal of faith, which is being carried out at a time when the farming population is on its knees and the economic conditions for farmers in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta are as devastating and desperate as they have ever been.

March 19, 1993
Government Orders
I cannot understand the heartlessness with which these promises have been broken. I cannot understand the lack of compassion and economic sense which is involved in breaking these promises because everybody who analyses the history economically knows that when our farm communities in western Canada have done well, this country has done well.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the chance to put these comments on the record. I hope the government will accept some of our amendments to eliminate some of the broken promises that it intends to put in place with respect to the WGTA.

Mr. Speaker, I want to add a point in the debate regarding western transportation, the original Crow rate and the subsequent western grain rate that replaced it.
I want to explain why, as a person with no direct contact with grain farming in the west or even in Ontario, I feel very strongly on this point, along with the rest of the NDP.
I grew up thinking that I was growing up in an agricultural country, a country that produced food to feed its people and even food to sell to the rest of the world. In the last few years I have begun to wonder when I found that farmers are being forced off the land. It happened when I was a kid during the depression. It happened partly because of a massive drought in the west and also because, as one old farmer said to me bitterly, they were selling their beef at one cent a pound in the depression.
But it is happening again without massive drought, without a world-wide depression of the same sort, but with something like a depression, with deliberate restructuring ol the economy of North America and other places by a few very powerful companies such as Cargill. These companies have great power to influence the decisions of government in their favour.
It is no longer certain that the land of Canada will feed the people of Canada. That might sound fantastic and ridiculous but for 15 years I have grown concerned about that when I learned Canada was exporting more and more beef cattle and hogs, and importing more and more sides of meat from as far away as Australia.
I began to wonder if we would lose the ability for Canadians to feed Canadians. Then I thought of what I
Mexico is a closer example. In the last 10 or 12 years the Mexican people have been eating less food. The consumption of food in Mexico has decreased by one-third. They eat only two-thirds as much food as they used to eat around 1980. This is not because the population has shrunk, if anything it has grown. But they eat less food.
One-third of the food they do eat is imported. What went before that was the gradual year by year destruction of the family farm, the campesino. The ejido, the communal lands protected by the Constitution, enabled a large number of Mexican campesino or farmers to produce the corn, rice, and beans they needed, plus a little over to sell to the people in the cities.
Those people are being forced off their land by changes in the Constitution brought about by Salinas at the direction of international capital so that the farmers will be pushed off their land. The Government of Mexico has reduced the subsidies to the farmers for irrigation, herbicides, pesticides and farm equipment. They can no longer compete with imported corn.
Corn grown in Iowa in the United States sells in Mexico for less than the price that the campecinos must charge in order to live because the United States subsidizes Iowa corn at $12 billion per year. This is more than the whole budget of the department of agriculture in Mexico.
Those farmers are being forced off their land in Mexico. Farmers are being forced off their land in Canada. It is not by drought or world-wide depression, but by the decisions of large corporations and by the decision of this government. This government is forcing farmers off their land by reducing the possibility of
March 19, 1993

farmers being paid what it costs to produce and sell wheat. It is forcing them to leave the land.
The beneficiary will be the great American-based corporations such as Cargill that will take over the land as corporation farms. Then they will be able to raise the price of wheat, flour and bread to anything they please in Canada. They will control the supplies in Canada. They will control the supplies that we can import from the United States or anywhere else. They will be able to push the price of basic food in Canada sky-high.
This government through legislation like this is giving them the opportunity to do this. This government is giving away the birthright of Canadians. It is giving away the control of our best farm land by raising the transportation costs the farmers must pay.
This government signed an unequal treaty with the United States which says that the United States can subsidize the Mississippi transportation system to 100 per cent and take Canadian grain down to New Orleans. But Canada cannot subsidize the transportation of grain through Canada to the west coast or the east coast.
One simple little gimmick does it. It is because the United States treats the Mississippi as a military installation, maintained by the U.S. Army Engineering Corps and therefore a subsidy is not a subsidy. However, Canada is prevented from doing anything similar.
It is clearly the United States which has directed the Government of Canada to introduce this disastrous law. It will have the effect of destroying a great many more family farms in Canada. Eventually Canadians will pay intolerable prices for the flour and bread produced. The price will be controlled from outside Canada by companies that have no interest in whether Canadian farmers can farm or whether Canadians can eat.
Shame on this government.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to debate this very important topic. The member from Trinity-Spadina eloquently pinned it down in his speech. What we are talking about is the cost of food and the supply of food.
Government Orders
What could be more important? What could be more important to a country with a traditional agricultural past like Canada has? What could be more important for a country than to be independent?
I know the independence of this country is slipping away. People sense that. That is the problem the Conservatives are going to have in their leadership campaign. It will come up in their attempt to hang onto office. They are not going to make it because they have basically been giving away this country piece by piece and people sense that. People want new policies to protect Canada.
Liberal policies.

My friend says Liberal policies. No, not Liberal policies because in this very issue talking about the Crow rate and transportation rates, I was in the House when the Liberals brought in the changes. They started it. I remember that debate well.
The member for Essex-Windsor paid tribute to one of our great colleagues here in the House, the member for Regina-Lumsden. I recall his leading us; he was leading the pack. We started as a dishevelled pack but ended up being pretty effective at the end of that debate.
I vividly recall the debate and I recall the contribution of the member for Regina-Lumsden. He led the debate and taught me at the time a little bit about farm economics. For someone who represents a suburban riding in British Columbia that was important. There were a lot of details about the Crow rate. We went through all the details, up and down the details.
The thing that sticks in my mind is basically what the member for Trinity-Spadina was getting at. The member for Trinity-Spadina represents an urban riding, right downtown. What he was getting at is that we people from urban and suburban ridings have to understand that it is important to protect the family farm and farmers in Canada. If we do not it will mean in the long run that people from outside this country will control our farms and the price of our food. We cannot really have an independent country if we have that.

At first it sounds good that it is a new global economy and we have to make changes in the old way Canada was operating. However, there is a limit to what those changes could be.
If we get rid of the family farm for big, corporate, foreign-controlled farms, we are not going to have control over future farming in Canada. People will say to someone on the west coast and this is happening now in the Port of Vancouver: "Well, we are just going to let some of that grain go down to Seattle or we will let some goods that are being shipped be picked up by trucks south of Alberta or south of British Columbia and connect it through that way. The lesson is this talk of: "Well, it is all in the global economy".
As the member for Trinity-Spadina pointed out, the Americans are subsidizing the Mississippi route, giving $12 billion to their farmers, more than the entire budget of the poor Mexican department of agriculture. Let us get into the real world and forget the propaganda.
In the real world one has to fight for survival and that is why Canada has been a great country. The Conservatives under Sir John A. Macdonald, a man for whom I might have even voted, he being a Scotsman, a lawyer, a good speaker and besides, the New Democratic Party was not around in 1867, had a national vision of Canada. He had a national policy. The policy was to link the east and the west. This government is de-linking it, making it north and south. Eventually it is going to join Canada with the United States. That is the agenda. That is the corporate agenda, to sell the country out so we will no longer have a country.
People wonder why NDP members get up and fight these battles. It is because we love Canada. We are getting into these fights in this battle over changes in the transportation subsidies and in the way we deal with our farmers in Canada.
People ask: "Why are you standing up to support the Canadian farmer? You are from the west coast". My answer is that the fate of my constituents on the west coast is tied to the fate of the Canadian farmers. Their survival is tied to the survival of my constituents and their jobs.
The New Democratic Party is the only party so far in this coming election to have put forward a job creation strategy. It is out there for everybody to see.

I challenge the members in the leadership to put out some policy so all Canadians can see it. Bill Clinton did that when he ran for President of the United States. He actually put out some policy. He said to people-

He said: Mr. Speaker, the intention of this bill is that as a result of the Minister of Finance's economic statement, the Minister of Employment and Immigration will bring the expenditures of the bill under control. This is something that I very strenuously differ with. The expenditures of the Unemployment Insurance Commission are out of control, not as a result of the unemployed but as a result of the economic policies of this government.
The purpose of my amendments is to attempt to bring some sensitivity and some sense to the changes within the UI portion of Bill C-113.
There has been an awful lot of emphasis put on voluntarily leaving one's employment and relating that to just cause. For the record, I would like to read into the record the definition of the word voluntary. I got this definition from the dictionary. It says that voluntary is: "done, acting, able to act of one's own free will, not constrained or compulsory, intentional". That is the definition.
Given that definition, I do not think that there is anyone in Canada today who leaves his or her job voluntarily. Everyone has a reason for leaving his or her job.
The problem is that it is a good reason, but according to the commission and the act it may not be a just cause reason. The onus and burden of proving that just cause is on the backs of the unemployed.
We have at our disposal a document that I have called a "but book". It describes a situation in which a person has just cause to leave his or her employment, but there are many conditions that must be met. This "but book"
March 19, 1993

now has been transposed and it has been put into this grey bible that we received from the commission.
I would just like to refer to it for a moment as it pertains to the case of sexual or other harassment. It states, among other things on the page, and rightfully so, that harassment of any kind is unacceptable, whether of a sexual nature or otherwise, intimidation, threats, blackmail, abuse of authority or poisoned work environment, whether by superiors or co-workers. I agree with that whole-heartedly, but the part that follows is what causes me some concern.
This grey bible lists reasonable alternatives for an employee who is sexually or otherwise harassed to follow. That is where the problem lies. As an alternative, a person who is sexually harassed must speak to the employer. If that employer happens to be the person who is doing the harassing then how can this employee be expected to face that employer? If the employer is despicable enough to be sexually harassing an employee how can that employee in all good faith go to that employer and say that the employer has to stop it? That will only cause more harassment.
People must explore the possibility of a transfer to another unit. If the employer is the person who is causing the harassment does anyone think for one minute that the employer is going to be willing to transfer people, to say that they are right, he has been harassing them so he will transfer them to another unit. Does anyone really think that is going to happen? I do not think so.
They must seek assistance of the union or association. They must follow the grievance procedure. They must use the provisions of the collective agreement. They must go through all of this process prior to proving just cause.
On the same page, under the title of Just Cause, it says: "No other reasonable alternative to quitting. Existing reasonable alternatives cannot resolve the situation. The harassment is intolerable for any period of time. Not necessary to undertake or to await the result of a tribunal hearing in respect to the employment or human rights". That last part causes some problems not only for me but for the agents who are hearing the evidence put to them as it relates to just cause for sexual harassment.
