It is not necessary to undertake or await the result of a tribunal hearing.
When we look through this grey bible we can see that every section relates to what the claimant must do. I would like to relate some of the cases for applying just cause. There is a case of an employee who is 18 years old and is being harassed by her employer to do more work. She must tolerate shift changes on very short or no notice at all. The claimant worked from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. in a gas station. She worked from 3 p.m. to 11 p.m. in the kitchen and she worked from 6 a.m. to 2 p.m., also in the kitchen.
The case is too long to read all its parts, but the point is, and it is not the only part that involves this case, it is a matter of this employee not having the ability to even correspond with her employer. She tried to speak to the employer but he was not there. She tried to speak to the kitchen manager but that person was not there on numerous occasions, so she finally had to tell her co-worker that she was leaving.
The adjudicator or the agent who saw this case said that this employee did not have just cause for leaving her employment and as a result disqualified her for nine weeks and reduced her benefits to 50 per cent.
When we look at numerous cases and talk about people leaving their employment for various reasons one wonders, when we talk about the jurisprudence and we talk about the 40 just cause reasons, as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Employment and Immigration referred to them, we can cite time after time various cases in which people have been harassed.
Here is another one. It concerns a 45-year old woman. The agent says: "According to the information presented with your claim for benefit you voluntarily left your job without just cause. You are therefore disqualified from receiving UI benefits for seven weeks and you will get a reduction in your benefits to 50 per cent".
If we look at the evidence there are three and one-half pages of written testimony from this 45-year old woman who was sworn at and told that she was despicable and did not know how to dress properly. She was put under such stress that her blood pressure soared to 220 over 150. She was told if she did not quit she was headed for a stroke or maybe a heart attack.

March 19, 1993
Government Orders
There is half a page from the employer that says: "In closing, I feel the remarks made about myself go beyond the sour grapes of a disgruntled employee and I will be forwarding a copy to my lawyer for an opinion on my legal rights".
This is clearly a case in which an employee made a claim to an agent and said: "I had to quit, I have no other recourse". The information was made available to the employer, and now the employer is going to seek legal action.
To add insult to injury, this woman lost benefits for seven weeks and her benefits were reduced to 50 per cent. Is that just cause? What determines just cause?
When we talk about the problems that exist today and when I look at legislation, I look for legislation that will make things better for people, that will do what it is supposed to do.
Allow me to quote a letter from the Attorney General addressed to myself dated March 5, 1993 in keeping with what I have been saying, which is that the decisions by adjudicators, by agents are inconsistent and that the 40 reasons of which we have heard are not being applied. Mr. Speaker, please allow me two quick remarks on that point to emphasize what I am saying.
The Attorney General says: "In paragraph 3.188 of the 1991 annual report we further reported that penalties were still applied inconsistently". He goes on to say: "As you can appreciate the application of penalties requires close monitoring and as such is an ongoing concern of the commission".
I also have a copy of a letter that was addressed to the chairman of the legislative committee that heard our arguments in regard to this legislation. It is from an employee representative on a hearing commission. In the letter this officer states: "I have heard reference to 40 reasons that will be allowed. I do not know what they are and if 40 reasons are contemplated then the public has a right to know what you are considering and I request a copy".
Mr. Speaker, I know you are being very generous and I appreciate that. My point is that my amendments would include those 40 reasons in the legislation, and would include a common law spouse. I am told the policy is that they are accepted, but it is not in the legislation.
My amendments are friendly amendments. In the strongest terms I urge everyone to support these amendments and I do thank you for your indulgence, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Marc Robitaille (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to comment on the motions presented by the hon. member for Timmins- Chapleau.
I would like to consider these motions one by one and comment accordingly. Motions Nos. 7 and 8 standing in the name of the hon. member are actually an attempt to expand the definition of just cause. This definition is found in clause 18 of the bill. Although there is no objection to the motion as such, the motion is unnecessary because the 13 reasons listed under clause 18 of the bill already cover the vast majority of the additional reasons proposed by the hon. member. I will remind hon. members that paragraph 28(4)(n) of clause 18 allows for prescribing regulations, which could easily serve the same purpose as the changes proposed by the hon. member.
Finally, all the reasons proposed by the hon. member are already part of the jurisprudence and, as such, are binding on the commission's officers, who must take these into account when making their decision. Unemployment Insurance officers cannot ignore the forty or fifty reasons recognized in the jurisprudence when they make a decision on the eligibility of a claimant.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to comment briefly on motion No. 9. It would require from the commission a standard of proof applicable to criminal cases "beyond any reasonable doubt". I may remind the hon. member that the Unemployment Insurance Act is social legislation, not criminal legislation providing for punishment, as does the Criminal Code. That is why I cannot support this motion.
Motion No. 10 proposes to include in the Unemployment Insurance Act a definition of the term spouse that adds the concept of common law spouse. I admit that the principle which inspired the hon. member for Timmins- Chapleau is sound, but I cannot support this motion
March 19, 1993

because it is not entirely necessary. Practically speaking, people who have lived together for at least one year are already treated as spouses according to UIC policy. In this respect, I may refer the hon. member to page G-45, chapter 6 of the guide. I would be delighted to send him a copy if he is interested.
I will now consider motions Nos. 11 and 13. There are two objectives here: first, to reinstate the system that existed prior to Bill C-113, and second, to introduce a three-stage disqualification system which would be based on the claimant's record of disqualification.
Even if these motions did not exceed the scope of this bill, I would object in any case, since the government has made it clear that individuals who leave a job voluntarily and without just cause should not have access to unemployment insurance benefits. These two motions would destroy the principle of the bill, and this of course means they are entirely unacceptable.
Finally, Motion No. 14 would provide that individuals leaving a job without just cause would be able to use the weeks of insurable employment preceding their voluntary departure to qualify again for benefits. This motion would lead to situations where individuals would leave a job without any penalty whatsoever. You will understand why the government cannot accept this motion.
As for the matter raised by the hon. member concerning sexual harassment, there are a few things I would like to say. The only reasonable alternative does not mean that the employee must speak to the employer if she is harassed. That would only be the case if the harassment came from someone else. It means the employee must at least make an effort to correct the situation, if at all possible. In some cases, the individual will not have to speak to the employer.
When there is just cause, there is nevertheless a procedure that says the employee must make a reasonable attempt to correct the situation. This applies to all cases of just cause. An attempt must be made at one's place of work to correct the situation. If that is impossible, then there is just cause because the situation cannot be changed. This also applies to sexual harassment.
Government Orders
In concluding, I would like to go back briefly to the motion which deals with the definition of common law spouse. I repeat, the principle which inspired the hon. member has great merit, but in practice, unemployment insurance officers have specific guidelines that provide that a common law spouse is to be treated as a spouse in the meaning of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Therefore it is unnecessary to have a debate on an amendment that is redundant and unnecessary, since in practice, the treatment of these cases is already fair and equitable.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you and I thank the member for Timmins-Chapleau for his amendment.
We have heard debate on both sides of this amendment. I want to put this amendment in the context of the bill and give a few ideas I have dealing specifically with the amendment but also with the bill in general.
What we are talking about here are changes to the UI program which are included in Bill C-113. These were first proposed by the Minister of Finance on December 2 here in the House of Commons. The changes involved the following: That the new UI benefit rate for new beneficiaries would be reduced from 60 per cent to 57 per cent of insurable earnings as of April 1, 1993, which is just a few days away; second, and this is the contentious issue, that people who voluntarily leave their jobs without just cause, as defined by section 28 of the UI Act, or lose their jobs through personal misconduct will no longer receive UI benefits.
Let us put that into the context of the state of the UI fund. You will see what effect it is going to have. There are a few people in this House and in Canada who know that the unemployment insurance program is the federal government's single largest expenditure for 1993 of almost $22 billion.
What does that mean? It means that more money is spent on the UI program than on national defence, Old Age Security or the total administration of the federal government. That is what we are dealing with here today.

March 19, 1993
Government Orders
Before 1990 the federal government's contribution to the UI fund was about 20 per cent. In 1990 the government decided that general revenues would no longer contribute to the UI fund. How was it going to do it then? The fund was going to be financed by UI premiums paid by employees and employers.
How did it raise all this money? These premiums have been raised since 1990, first by a 24 per cent increase in July 1991 and then by another 7.1 per cent increase in January 1992. Revenues collected from these premiums totalled almost $18 billion for 1992-93. Despite such revenues the cost of the program has climbed $7 billion since 1990.
Why? It is due in large part to an unemployment rate which has gone from 8.1 per cent in 1990 to 10.3 per cent in 1991 to 11.3 in 1992. I think in fairness that we have to say that this could be directly attributable to the policies of the present government. Because of the steadily rising UI costs the UI fund is in a deficit position. The cumulative deficit is $4.9 billion.
With that as a background, just what effect will the changes in Bill C-113 have on the UI fund? Surely if we are going to make changes they will tend to clear up the deficit. Let us have a look at some of the figures.
The government expects that cutting the benefit rate from 60 per cent to 57 per cent and eliminating UI benefits for voluntary leavers and those who are fired from their jobs will save a total of $2.5 billion over two years. Nonetheless, even with these cuts the deficit in the UI fund is expected to rise to $7.6 billion by the end of 1993. That is up from $4.9 billion now, as we speak.
It is clear therefore that the effect of the changes in Bill C-113 will be negligible. If the purpose of the government in introducing these changes was to control spending as was stated by the minister in December 1992, it can be said in fairness that the government has failed.
We have to ask another question. What effect will these changes have on Canadian society? It has been shown that the measures proposed in this bill will not reduce or even contain a deficit of the UI fund. It is also clear that the changes do not target cheaters and by
going after quitters the restrictions are aimed at a relatively small section of the UI recipients.
It is safe to say therefore that the government in this instance is simply cutting for the sake of cutting without any all-encompassing vision of what the UI program should be doing and without any idea of how the program could be made to work better.
The stated purpose of hunting down and punishing quitters is nothing more than a convenient fiction used to distract people from the real issue. The government does not know what to do about Canada's unemployment crisis and that is the real problem. Unfortunately the price to be paid by society in general for these relatively inconsequential and ineffective cuts could be quite high.
In 1990 the government enacted the latest UI restrictions and thousands of families were thrown into poverty. The percentage of unemployed workers covered by the program dropped from 70 per cent to 58 per cent. Where did these people go? They had to eat. They had to live some place. They had to keep their families going.
If the proposed changes in this bill become law those people no longer eligible for unemployment insurance will have to turn to the already overtaxed welfare system that is for the most part covered by the cities.
The Conservatives, this government, have clearly decided to attack the unemployed rather than attack the scourge of unemployment. Under this proposal Canadians will bear the burden of proof in establishing their just cause for leaving their jobs.
In 1986 I recall the Conservatives established the Forget commission which presented recommendations which would have gutted the UI system as we know it. However, even Claude Forget, the head of the study questions the Tory measures calling them "a political miscalculation and economically just an empty gesture, a waste of time and of political credibility".
Not even their ideological soul mates are with the Conservatives on these measures. The measure dealing with just cause will discourage legitimate complaints about sexual harassment and substandard working conditions.
March 19, 1993

Immigrant women and non-unionized workers will be even more vulnerable at the work place as a result of these changes. The government should not support measures which chain a worker to a particular job regardless of the treatment received from an employer. This is Canada. This is 1993. We are not at the stage where we used to have people come over in servitude. Surely in this day and age we can be a little more compassionate with our Canadian confreres.
The UI program is designed to provide income replacement and to promote labour flexibility and mobility. Many people will be discouraged from seeking better employment opportunities for themselves given this punitive and Draconian measure. Many workers will be forced to stay at low paying and dead end jobs. Is that what we want for our Canadian workers? I suggest it is not.
If this legislation passes the UI system could find itself buried under an avalanche of appeals, literally hundreds of thousands of appeals. In 1991, 191,000 UI applicants were held to have quit their jobs without just cause and were penalized. About 19,000 of these rulings were reversed. Why if everything was so fair and above board?
Resources of the department are stretched in dealing with this level of appeals. It is ludicrous to believe that a department could cope with 190,000 appeals. Should it attempt to do so? It is entirely likely the standards of just cause will be applied in an inconsistent and arbitrary fashion.
I remember the police, the squealer police or whatever they are called. If we thought our neighbours were doing wrong we would call the police: send in the cops and make sure they were punished and penalized for losing their jobs or leaving a job they could not stand.
We have come a long way since 1984. A 1991 Economic Council of Canada report found that people who quit their jobs were not a drain on the UI fund. In an analysis of 1986 the unemployed figures show that half of all job quitters went to another job immediately. Another 43 per cent found new jobs within 10 weeks. By contrast, one in five persons who lost their jobs found work immediately and another 50 per cent had found work within 10 weeks.
Government Orders
I know that time is running short. I want to leave this thought with the House. The people of Canada want to work. They want good paying jobs to support themselves and their families. I suggest to the House that if this bill is passed it will call into question the honest, hard working people of Canada who in a time of need had the Government turn its back on them and literally throw them on to the welfare rolls.

Mr. Speaker, shame on the government. It is sad to say we are debating a bill that does not have one redeeming factor.
As I said earlier when I spoke on the bill, not only does it attack unemployed workers when they are down, when they are hurting the most, when they are faced with double digit unemployment, it attacks Public Service workers who work for the unemployed in unemployment centres. We have workers who for economic reasons, because of failed economic policies of this government, are unemployed and on unemployment insurance. They are now being penalized, harassed and threatened. They are guilty until they can prove their innocence. We also have public sector workers whose wages have been frozen, who have to work in understaffed UI centres and somehow have to accommodate and work with angry unemployed workers whose benefits are being yanked back by the government. We have two sets of workers this government is managing to mesh into one piece of legislation.
I want to address most of my remarks to the additional clauses introduced by the UI critic for my party, the member for Timmins-Chapleau, concerning legitimate just cause. The hon. member pointed out that the government had touted 40 reasons why one could quit a job but in fact spelled out less than half of them in the bill. Why would that be? Are 27 of the reasons secret? Do we have secret reasons and public reasons? Why would the government not have included all 40 reasons in the bill rather than only 13 of them?
A lucky number.

Lucky number 13 is not so lucky for the workers of Canada, but maybe the government figures it is a lucky number.

March 19, 1993
Government Orders
I want to address some of the reasons the hon. member has added in his amendment, such as a formal promise of increase in wages or salary that was not fulfilled. Formal promise is equal to a contract. If somebody breaks a contract is that not just cause for leaving the work place? Or, are we setting up a situation wherein the government is providing a scenario so that the employer can now renege on agreements and know that the worker cannot make a move because the worker will not be able to collect unemployment insurance if the employer does not live up to his end of the agreement?
The second reason that the hon. member has in his amendment is unjustified reduction in wages or salary. That is not just cause for leaving a work place, a wage cut. A worker goes to work with a commitment that he or she will receive certain compensation for doing that work. Now the scenario is that an employer can say arbitrarily: "You will take a wage cut. You have nowhere to go because unemployment insurance is cut off for you". Shame.
Loss in wages or salary due to the employer's financial difficulty is another reason. What can the employer do if he or she has financial difficulty? There are several remedies the employer could seek. The employer could seek funding from financial institutions. The employer could seek bankruptcy. It is not pleasant but it is available to an employer. An employer could in fact cut workers' wages. What does the worker have to do? The worker has no options because he or she is caught again by this bill which leaves him or her guilty of something if he or she withdraws his or her labour.
Intolerable working conditions, unreasonable work requirements, wages or salaries that are less than provided for by legislation, or an employer who does not pay minimum wage are other reasons. A worker has to stay there and work because the government says that worker has no right to unemployment insurance. It is shameful.
Moral objections to the employer's illegal activities or employer's activities that violate freedom of conscience are not cause under the Unemployment Insurance Act for quitting a job. Place of work distant from family and serious sickness in the family are not causes under the Unemployment Insurance Act to quit a job.
Exertion by employer of excessive pressures to retire is not cause to collect unemployment insurance any more. In this economic climate many employers are putting pressure on older workers to retire.
Working conditions that in the opinion of a medical practitioner adversely affect the person's health are not cause under this bill to quit a job. Shame. A doctor says this job is going to kill you but this government says you have to stay in it because it will not give you unemployment insurance while you seek another job. It is shameful.
Working conditions considered on credible and convincing explanations by the claimant as adversely affecting the claimant's health are not just cause. Again, too bad about the employee's health. The government says the employee has to keep working and cannot collect unemployment insurance.
Long periods of separation from family due to distance of place of work from family residence is not just cause. This is a country where we have all kinds of industry with camp living: fly in and fly out. Marriages can hardly survive. They have very tough times surviving because the workers have to leave home for long periods of time. We could even say that for members of Parliament. We know about fly in and fly out work conditions and how tough it is to keep the family together. But it is too bad for workers. It is not just cause to leave a job to try to save a marriage, to save a family, and be at home with kids who are having problems. Those are not just causes under this government legislation.
If the government really thought about the conditions being created for Canadian workers and what it was really saying to Canadian workers, after sober reflection it would probably withdraw this bill with a whole bunch of shame. The government's attitude is: if you quit your job in this country you are a cheat; if you quit your job in this country you want to go skiing; if you quit your job in this country you are lazy or if you quit your job in this country you are guilty until you are proven innocent.
If that is what a Tory Canada is all about, I would suggest the government had better hasten its way to the electoral ballot box. I do not believe most Canadians
.fe
March 19, 1993

think this is what our Canada is about. I suspect there may be a change of heart when the election comes and the government finds itself with a bunch of amendments as it sits in opposition. Then we will amend this bill so the workers of Canada are treated with dignity and respect and are innocent until proven guilty.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to talk about men and women who have left their jobs voluntarily and about the fact that this bill proposes they should not receive any unemployment insurance benefits if they left without a good reason.

What I have discovered in discussing this bill and the new penalty provision with many of my constituents is that the presentation of the issue, I suppose particularly by the minister, has resulted in a great deal of misunderstanding among the general public about what the existing rules are for unemployment insurance in the event people leave their jobs voluntarily without just cause.
The minister through his rhetoric has managed to convey to many Canadians the notion that lots and lots of people are quitting their jobs, that this fact is causing a large expenditure of public money, and that unless this bill is brought in these people will simply get UI without problem and very easily.
Many constituents to whom I have spoken have the notion that people who quit their jobs voluntarily are not at the moment subject to any penalty for doing so. That impression in itself is not correct. The existing law provides for a penalty of a minimum of seven and a maximum of twelve weeks without benefits in the event of somebody quitting a job without just cause.
Surely the starting point is that Canadians need to understand this is a phenomenon subject to penalty already and it is not necessary to have this particular bill passed to penalize people who quit their jobs without just cause.
The second notion is that these quitters are causing a major drain on the fund. It is important to understand that the number of people who actually quit their jobs is relatively limited and has been declining over past years. In fact the number who quit their jobs at the peak of the
Government Orders
economic cycle in 1988 was much higher than now. This reflects the fact that people do not quit their jobs readily when they know times are tough. They may be more inclined to do so when they are better able to find another job. According to a 1991 Economic Council of Canada report, about half the people who quit their jobs voluntarily do so to go to other jobs. About 43 per cent of the remainder find new jobs within 10 weeks.
We also know, according to the Economic Council of Canada, may it rest in peace, only 1.5 per cent to 1.7 per cent of the unemployment rate consists of people who left their jobs voluntarily. The notion that this is the remedy for the UI deficit is ridiculous. That is just not the point.
The next thing I want to raise so people understand is that the existing system of a penalty of seven to twelve weeks where people quit their jobs without just cause provides, for the adjudicator of unemployment insurance claims, the ability to weigh the merits of the reasons for quitting their jobs, consider their credibility in making the statements made for giving reasons, and judge what the appropriate penalty should be.
When people come in and say they are applying for UI benefits because they quit their jobs, the first stage is to determine whether or not they had just cause. The second stage is if they did not have just cause, what degree of penalty is appropriate in that case. That is the existing law. When the UI law was initially reformed in a major way in 1971, the penalty for quitting a job was one to three weeks. It was later increased to a maximum of six weeks. It was then increased to a minimum of seven and a maximum of twelve.
Although it changed throughout that period of time, there was always a discretion involved in determining what the appropriate period of disqualification was.
This bill has made a major change in that, not just by increasing the extent of the penalty but by narrowing the discretion to one which must be exercised either in favour of the claimant by saying yes this person quit with just cause, in which case no penalty is applicable, or at the other extreme this person did not have just cause and the penalty is no benefits whatsoever. It is sort of the capital punishment of unemployment insurance penalties.

Government Orders
The essence of mitigation, of figuring out whether somebody took appropriate steps in the circumstances, or tried to but gave to the insurance officer an ability to use some discretion, is lost. To my mind it entirely undermines a system on which years of jurisprudence have accumulated in determining what is just cause and what is the appropriate degree of penalty that should be meted out to somebody who quits his or her job.
I did not bother to bring in the decisions of the unemployment insurance umpire and the Federal Court on this issue. It is sufficient to say there is a large range of cases that have dealt with issues of voluntary quitting or dismissal for misconduct and determinations made as to what the appropriate penalty was.
What we do know is that under the existing system in which the penalty period is a range of weeks of disqualification from seven to twelve, the average penalty given to people who are found to have quit voluntarily without just cause is just over eight weeks. In other words, the average penalty is close to the minimum one.
It reflects the fact that adjudicators under the Unemployment Insurance Act, in considering whether people have just cause to quit, usually come to the conclusion that although they did not have sufficient cause to quit, they did have good enough reasons to lessen the degree of penalty being prescribed. Even with that there are a lot of appeals.
Consider this point. Put yourself in the position of the adjudicator of an unemployment insurance claim for leaving a job voluntarily. Your choice as adjudicator is this. Does this claimant get benefits or no benefits, full benefits or no benefits? Under this bill that remains to be the choice.
I suggest that most adjudicators, if they can find a shred of justification for people quitting, are probably going to give them benefits. I know this may even differ from what some of my colleagues have said.
Even looking at it from the point of view of the government's attempt to justify this on fiscal grounds, it just does not make sense. If they lean the other way and refuse benefits, because the penalty is that severe they virtually ensure that there will be an appeal.
I tell you, Mr. Speaker, in the unemployment insurance administration the processing of appeals is a very expensive one because a panel must be brought together. The panel members are not regular employees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. They are paid a fee for the day. They have to be given briefs of what the law is. They have to be given all the facts of the case. By creating this mechanism, the government has stood fiscal responsibility on its head.
Why has the government done that? Other than out of sheer stupidity, I suggest it is because in fact we are right. It is trying to go out and appeal to a right wing constituency in Canada by misleading them into thinking that there are thousands and thousands of people quitting their jobs without just cause and it has to put a stop to that. It is not true.
What the government is doing is fiscally irresponsible. It is unfair, it is unjust, it is against the traditions of our system of justice, it is wrong and it should be stopped.

Mr. Speaker, I am of two minds rising to speak on this bill this afternoon. On the one hand I am as always delighted to partake in debate here. On the other hand, I really am sick at heart at what has been done to the working people once again by their government.
March 19, 1993

I have some notes on this bill and in black print above the second list of notes are the words "guilty until proven innocent". Those words are the complete antithesis of our belief in law in this country.
We refer to the problem of a person before our courts who is considered guilty until proven innocent as the reverse onus. That reverse onus has in a number of cases before the Supreme Court of Canada relating to the criminal law been thrown out, so far, I might add, that it has bounced into obscurity. In Bill C-113 we are right back to a reverse onus against the people who are least able to defend themselves.
It is a reverse onus against workers who will be thrown out of jobs, who have no money and no back-up, who cannot afford recourse to lawyers. Because of other cuts by the government, the legal aid offices in this country from coast to coast to coast no longer take the kinds of civil cases these amendments would engender. It is a disgrace and a scandal.
I cannot believe people good and true on the government side of the House can support this. I cannot believe first and foremost the scam that is being perpetrated on the people of Canada with regard to the whole question of sexual harassment under this bill.
This week we have had a number of questions in this House put to the members of the government on the question of sexual harassment. I have heard time and again from the Minister Responsible for the Status of Women, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Labour, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the President of the Treasury Board and again and again from the Prime Minister, and what have I heard? I have heard the words that this government has zero tolerance for sexual harassment. Well, talk is cheap. Words are pretty. Actions are what we need here, action that proves that sentence.
Now, my learned and dear friend from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso just said, and I am going to quote him: "What this government has," and I agree with him, "is zero tolerance for Canadians". Very soon Canadians are going to have zero tolerance of their own.
The whole question of this bill vis-a-vis the question of sexual harassment has snowballed to the point where
Government Orders
women and men of goodwill are asking: "What is the government doing?"
Time and again the situation has been explained by members on this side of the House to the minister of employment, the Prime Minister and the Minister Responsible for the Status of Women. It is as if ears are filled with wet cement. They are not hearing what we are saying and if they are hearing, they certainly are not understanding.
The cement goes deeper than that.

True. The hon. member for Timmins- Chapleau says the cement goes deeper than that and he is right. This is a very serious matter, this question of sexual harassment and how it is affects women in this country.
Years ago, between 1980 and 1984, I chaired the Unemployment Insurance Appeal Board in Halifax. I sat several days every month and listened to cases brought by working people who had been disqualified and penalized for a period in those days of from four to six weeks from receiving their UI benefits.
I discovered we had a very stringent bill and if people left their employment voluntarily, you were disqualified for a severe period of time. Eventually, as a result of the insurance nature of the scheme, the disqualification ended and they did receive benefits for a certain period of time.
The hardest thing to prove at that quasi-judicial committee was just cause in a voluntary quit. Now it is even more crucial that just cause be given the widest possible interpretation because women who claim they have been sexually harassed will have to prove it on the balance of probabilities or they will lose all their benefits. They will be disqualified and disentitled.
The same goes for other people, men and women both, who quit for other reasons. The onus will be on them to prove it.
The second problem is that the employer, who can be the best witness of a voluntary quit and just cause, is not compellable to these hearings. He does not have to come and testify. There is no power of subpoena. How are we going to get him there? Sorry about the pronoun but in most cases it is going to be a him.

Government Orders
What are we going to do? We cannot bring this person by compulsion to these hearings. We have a woman, in most cases, who probably makes $20,000 a year so she cannot afford legal representation. Legal aid offices are not taking cases like this anymore because of cutbacks from this government and other governments across the country.
The whole question of sexual harassment is very embarrassing and painful to a woman in the first place. She goes in and says she quit her job because her boss poisoned the work place or said that if she did not sleep with him, she would not get this promotion or would be fired, any one of two dozen possible scenarios that come under the realm of sexual harassment.
She gets to someone in Employment and Immigration Canada who says she has to prove it, and the civil burden of proof is on the balance of probabilities. It is not as strong as beyond a reasonable doubt, which is the criminal burden, but it is still a heavy burden that must be discharged and there is no help for her.
Over and over again I listened to the minister of employment say that sexual harassment is grounds for just cause. It may be just cause on paper but what about in practice? Practice is what we are dealing with.
I would be delighted to hear from any member of the government, from the minister of health on down, a scenario in which someone in that situation proved a just cause in a voluntary quit.
I would be happy and delighted. I promise I would eat crow from one end of this nation to the other. I would be happy to do that if anyone could show me a case in which a woman was able to prove just cause given the situation I set up: with a boss who is not compellable, with an Employment and Immigration Commission that says the burden of proof is on her, and with no recourse to legal counsel which is where most of them-
Oh, Oh.

If the minister would like to answer my question I would be delighted to hear him say it. Ah, shrug. Nice to see you.
I would be delighted to backtrack on this. I say here I will backtrack if anyone can show me a case in which a woman was able to prove that in those circumstances,
because sadly I know that is not possible. Sadly, if it is not possible now how much worse does the whole thing become when Bill C-113 becomes law and women are disentitled right off the top?
In a nutshell the problem is this with regard to sexual harassment. There is not a woman in the world who does not know what we are talking about. I have never had a problem explaining sexual harassment to a woman. I met with all sorts of groups yesterday and every time I talked about it the nods started. Women of good faith who were being honest, and in most cases they are.
There are two kinds of men. There are the men who indulge in this kind of activity. They do not want any more publicity about it so they deny it. Then there are the other men who are the majority of those who sit in this Chamber. They are good men who want to do the right thing, regardless of political affiliation. I believe that of the 295 of us, of the 255 men, the vast majority want to do the right thing. I believe that. I do not think I could stay here if I did not believe it.
The difficulty is that the whole question of sexual harassment is so foreign for most men that they cannot believe anybody does it. Gentlemen, we are here to say that it happens all the time. It happens everywhere.
I see my time is up. Let me just end with a plea. This bill is going to make it worse.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad of the chance to support the hon. member for Timmins-Chapleau on his motion in this matter because it is a very serious attack that is being made on a large number of working people in this country, hundreds of thousands by the government's statistics and many more than that potentially or by threat.
March 19, 1993

Working people are to be denied the unemployment insurance they have paid for if they quit under circumstances they consider justifiable, perhaps even under circumstances listed in the law but which they cannot prove because the rules by which they have to prove it are loaded in favour of the employer who may have forced them into quitting.
Some years ago I heard it said by a lawyer, who in fact was minister of justice in a provincial government, that union members are second class citizens in this country because they are the only ones who can be sent to jail for not working. If a doctor does not work or if a banker does not work they do not go to jail. A union member can.
At first I was surprised. Then of course I saw it happen.
I remember what Jean-Claude Parrot said about his experience. He said: "There seems to be two kinds of laws in this country. When the RCMP illegally opened the mail the government passed a law to make it legal. When workers legally go on strike it passes a law to make it illegal".
This law does not apply only to union members. It applies to all employees and potentially threatens every employee with being starved for lack of unemployment insurance if he or she takes the risk of quitting for what he or she believes is just cause.
The basic reason for that, which others have mentioned but which deserves to be emphasized again, is that the burden of proof is on the worker. It is not on the employer nor on the unemployment insurance system. He or she must prove by rules that have not been clearly stated what it was that gave grounds for quitting. In fact that person is guilty until proven innocent. Unless it can be proven that the person is innocent of the offence of quitting without just cause, then that person is treated as guilty.
This is in reverse of the general way the law is applied in our country, but there is a precedent. It is not applied to Canadian citizens or Canadian residents. It is applied to someone who has come to Canada and applied for refugee status. That person is treated from that moment as though he or she were a criminal or at least a violator of the Immigration Act. This would be until months or years later as the law drags its course and that person can prove that he or she really was a refugee and therefore
Government Orders
was not to be held guilty for entering the country without a valid visa.
In other words, the government tried it out first on people who were in Canada without the protection of either citizenship or Canadian residency. Having made it work there in the sense that it got away with it, the government is now trying it on every Canadian who is employed. If you quit you are guilty, unless you can prove you are innocent.
There are no clearly stated rules adopted by Parliament by which that is to be decided as there is in the case of criminal law. There are rules which can be changed at will by the cabinet. They may or may not be fully published. They may be left vague. There is nothing that the public, nothing that Parliament can do about those vague rules.
The person is deprived of income from the word go without anything to live on. This is until the person is able to prove he or she is innocent of quitting without due cause. This may be after months without legal aid.
There is no time limit for the UI system to give a decision. The UI system is not losing money. It is the worker who has to live without money. The unemployment insurance system does not care whether it takes two weeks, two months or two years to give a final decision on an appeal to an umpire.
I have a letter concerning a constituent in Trinity- Spadina. It is a very concise statement of her problem written by a person on her behalf. It reads:
"This person quit her job in November 1992. Her boss was an alcoholic and was verbally abusing her. She had 18 former employees as witnesses. Her claim was accepted at the unemployment insurance office; she was not penalized at all.
In January 1993, her former boss appealed the decision to the board of referees. This worker went to that hearing with three witnesses and five letters and the 18 names and phone numbers of former workers who were her friends and were willing to testify on her behalf. The referees did not question her witnesses at all. She was accused of stealing those 18 names and phone numbers from her boss's work place.
On February 11 a decision came down that she had good reason to quit but not just cause."

March 19, 1993
Private Members' Business
What gobbledegook. I know this government spends millions of dollars of taxpayers' money studying what words will con the public into thinking the government means what it does not mean by the words it uses. So having good reason to quit is not the same as having just cause. That is the kind of gobbledegook that a worker cannot be expected to foresee.
She is now penalized seven weeks and gets 50 per cent of her pay. She was lucky under the old system. She is appealing to the umpire. The lawyer believes she has a strong case. Her former boss also had former employees go to the Canadian Human Rights Commission and there has been no decision yet and to the Ontario Labour Relations Board which has ruled in his favour.
If she had the misfortune of having this happen to her after this present law she would not be losing just seven weeks. She would lose all her weeks and not know when she would ever get a decision on her appeal to the umpire.
This is a monstrously unjust law which victimizes workers for being workers, for being employees and not for being bosses.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say a very few words and allow my colleagues on both sides of the House to also say a few words on this bill. I would first indicate that the purpose of this bill is to designate November 20 of each year as national child day in order to promote in Canada an awareness of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child which was adopted in the United Nations General Assembly on November 20.
On behalf of Canada, as you know, Mr. Speaker, our Prime Minister chaired the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child and this bill continues this momentum. Before proceeding I would like to take this opportunity to thank many people who have made this bill a reality.
In particular I owe a deep thanks to Our Kids, Results Canada and the Coalition for the Rights of the Child, all of whom played an integral role in bringing the issue of child poverty to light.
Also I owe a special acknowledgement to Janis Ma-chin. Without her initiative, help and support this bill would never have got as far as it did.
Finally, I would like to recognize the support I have received from the House leaders of all parties on both sides of the House. In particular, I would like to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare and his department, my leader for his unwavering support and encouragement, and the many members of this House who have contacted my office to offer their support for Bill C-371.
March 19, 1993

The interest this bill has created certainly shows the importance that members from all parties in this House place on recognizing the importance of children.
Canada is recognized as being the number one country in the world in terms of social, economic and political stability and prosperity. Yet, unfortunately, we have over one million children who live in poverty. In fact, according to Statistics Canada, children now make up the single largest group of poor people in our country.
Children who live in poverty are at twice the risk of dying before reaching the age of 20. They have increased rates of chronic illness; they often suffer increased physical and mental disabilities and increased psychiatric disorders; and a greater percentage of poor children and youth struggle in school and face higher drop-out and illiteracy rates.
At a time when our children should experience the joy of growing up, learning and experiencing new things, many children unfortunately are left out.
This bill I believe takes a giant step forward in recognizing the many challenges the children and youth of our nation face today. By designating every November 20 as a national child day we are sending a signal to all Canadians that the issues affecting our youth are important to us all.
This bill ensures that once a year communities from coast to coast will stop and recognize children and the issues affecting them. We can ensure that every year we will pay tribute to the future of our great country Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to affirm my support and the support of the Minister of National Health and Welfare for this bill and to compliment my hon. colleague, the member for Ottawa Centre, for his initiative in bringing this bill forward.
Canadians will remember that our Prime Minister was an early supporter of the World Summit for Children and that when asked by UNICEF and member states of the United Nations to co-chair the summit, he accepted and that summit was an unqualified success.
Canadians will also remember that one of the subjects of the World Summit for Children was the Convention on the Rights of the Child and in the final communique
Private Members' Business
and the subsequent action plan endorsed by the 71 participating leaders, the ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child became the first commitment expected of governments around the world.
History will record that the Prime Minister returned to Canada from the world summit to fulfil his promise that the conditions of children must become a major issue on the political agenda in all countries. The Prime Minister created the Children's Bureau in October 1991, ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child in December 1991 and oversaw his government's introduction of Brighter Futures in May 1992. Let me take each of these accomplishments in turn.
A dedicated bureau within the Government of Canada to co-ordinate and reflect the interests of children in policy and program development was the recommendation of the International Year of the Child Committee in 1979. Today it exists in the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Canada has ratified the convention on the rights of the child. In a ceremony held here in the Parliament Buildings in the presence of children from all regions of Canada and members of the Canadian Coalition For the Rights of Children, the convention was signed by the Prime Minister. The convention on the rights of the child is very important to Canadians and I would like to take this opportunity to elaborate upon this point.
Children are exceptionally vulnerable. They require special rights to protect them and meet their unique needs. The convention, as an international legal agreement, provides us with a set of standards that confirms the respect our society gives its youngest members. The convention asserts the underlying principle that the best interest of the child should always be the primary consideration. It outlines the responsibility we have as legislators and parents. The convention asks us to look at children in a new way as people and citizens with the same inherent rights as all other members of the union family.
In the hustle of our daily lives, among the constant demands upon our time and energy, this is not easy nor is it simple. In creating this national day to draw attention to the convention, we are responding to article 42 of the convention. This article, one of the shortest of the 54

March 19, 1993
Private Members' Business
articles that make up the body of the convention, is one of the most powerful for the future well-being of children. It says: "States parties undertake to make the principles and provisions of the convention widely known by appropriate and active means to adults and children alike". This bill will help us accomplish this objective.
Under the Brighter Futures program, which I will speak about in a moment, the Government of Canada has embarked upon these important tasks of public awareness and involvement in the convention on the rights of the child. In partnership with Professional Publishing Associates, the publisher of several parenting magazines, including Today's Parent, a delightful booklet has been developed that parents can read with then-young children. This colourful booklet outlines, in appropriate language, the intent of the convention for children and parents. Over the coming months, over one million households with young children will be receiving this booklet.
The Department of Multiculturalism has produced a beautiful poster that voluntary organizations and professional publishing associates are distributing to children's hospitals, child care centres, parent resource centres and schools and parents. Over 40,000 copies will be provided. These two programs are part of a thoughtful effort to familiarize Canadians with the convention in a user-friendly way that involves children and their parents together. We must never forget that the convention speaks eloquently to the central importance of parents in the healthy upbringing of children. The convention safeguards this parental role by stressing that the state must respect the responsibilities, rights and duties of parents in providing appropriate direction and guidance. There will be many partners as we recognize the national day to recognize the convention and the children of Canada.
The Canadian Coalition For the Rights of Children, a coalition of over 45 national organizations, has written the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare expressing its support for a national day. The city of Ottawa anticipating this national day by a year, held a celebration of children last November 20 at a local school. The Government of Canada will welcome the date of November 20 as an annual day for children. By selecting November 20, this government will affirm a common national day around which Canadians, their
organizations and governments will mobilize their efforts to recognize the rights of children.
This bill is also consistent with the government's comprehensive program for children, called Brighter Futures. In fact, the convention on the rights of the child is the first of four components of Brighter Futures. The other three are the new child tax credit recently passed by this House, Canadian action plan for children and the Child Development Initiative. Taken together, these four components form a major commitment toward children by this government that totals approximately $2.6 billion over five years, and ongoing funding for many programs beyond the five years.
Brighter Futures is more than a program or list of activities. It is an idea and a way of thinking about children. The convention is the cornerstone, a set of standards that must be the ever-present guide to all we undertake on behalf of children. The child tax benefit supplement for low and middle income working parents is a new policy instrument that recognizes the serious economic pressures on many Canadian families as they raise their children. The action plan is an outline of the longer-term issues that must be addressed by Canadian society in order to constantly improve the conditions in which our children live and grow. The child development initiative is our confirmation that early involvement with children, particularly those growing up under conditions of risk, can change the outcomes of children for the better as they grow to adulthood.
.(1515)
Brighter Futures recognizes that in recent years a body of research on child development is shifting the focus of social policy for children from attempting to solve problems once they have disrupted the child's life, to anticipating and preventing them through timely intervention.
Increasingly we can see the pathways that lead to problems in later life and the influences that protect or buffer children. Positive influences include healthy pregnancies and birth weight, loving parents who are knowledgeable about child development, caring families and supportive communities. Relatively simple and early interventions are targeted that can help a child move from a dangerous pathway to a healthy pathway.
March 19, 1993

The programs that illustrate the idea of Brighter Futures are coming on line. A guide to Brighter Futures will be available in several weeks. It will describe over 20 separate initiatives within the child development initiative, all based on early investment in children and the prevention of conditions of risk.
I am proud of the progress begun by this government on behalf of children, beginning with the world summit just over two and a half years ago. I am conscious that this progress reflects the Prime Minister's interest in children.
I am delighted to express my support for the bill currently before the House. Children are important to all of us. Contributions to their well-being must be made by all of us. This bill adds to our society's recognition of the important place we must establish for children and is welcome.
I would like to add that as chair of the subcommittee on poverty we are preparing a system so that perhaps next November 20 we will be able to have some measures to help us assess our progress in combating child poverty.
I know the member for Ottawa Centre has been tabling petitions, as have many other members of this House and I. Indeed I was at the ceremony beginning the spreading of that petition. Members of this House have also passed a resolution to eliminate child poverty by the year 2000.
Our subcommittee is hard at work developing standards so we can assess the state that children are living in across the country and perhaps work to have national standards in welfare or a guaranteed annual income. That is also being discussed at the current moment, and a paper by the minister will be presented on it.
All Canadians want to see that children in this country have a standard of living that is acceptable and reasonable and that they all have the opportunity to thrive.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the bill because of children, not because of the hypocrisy that has come to this House with the presentation of the bill.
It is hypocritical to have a national child day without accompanying policy that sees an end to hungry children in this country. We have just heard the litany of things
Private Members' Business
the government has done and will do for children, a government that has reneged twice on a national child care program to make sure children are safe and secure while their parents works.
Forty per cent of those using food banks in this country are children under 16 years. We just debated today a policy that will create more families having to resort to food banks because they cannot get unemployment insurance and we have double-digit unemployment.
One million children live in poverty and yet the government member who just spoke from Don Valley North, the chair of the subcommittee for poverty, has recently said the poverty line should be lowered. Will this help children?
Seventy-four per cent of women in their child-bearing years are in the work force. Yet, as I said, there is a dramatic shortage of child care spaces.
Are our children not worth government attention when it comes to their safety and care while their parents are working? The government withdrew funding for the Kids Help Line, a national line designed to help children in crisis.
Now we have a proposed national child day. As I said we support anything that will improve the conditions of children but will a day, November 20, improve the conditions of children without policy?
Where is the Liberal policy on child care? It is the NDP government in Ontario and the federal NDP policy that has taken real positive steps to address the crisis in child care in Canada.
Marion Dewar, the national director of the Canadian Council on Children and Youth is a former member of this House. We hope with the support of the people from Ottawa Centre she will be a member of this House again. She has advocated for an end to child poverty for years. She said: "Spending money on child poverty is not an addition to deficit but an investment in the future".
It may interest those in this House and Canadians who are watching that the sponsor of this bill joined with the then mayor of Ottawa, Jim Durrell, in abolishing the Youth Advisory Council. That council provided a way for the needs of young people to be recognized in those programs delivered by the city of Ottawa.

March 19, 1993
Private Members' Business
There is considerable irony in the fact that here today the Liberal member is calling for a national child day. However, when pushed to put into action those policies that truly benefit children, we find the Liberals lacking and in fact, doing just the opposite to what this bill is all about.
I listened to a member from the Liberal benches on an open-line show in British Columbia. He talked about economic policies that would create even worse situations for children currently living in poverty.
On Monday, September 25, 1989, I introduced a private member's motion concerning a suggested child protection commission. It read: "That in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of negotiating with the provinces to provide a comprehensive bill of rights for children which would standardize laws throughout the country and that this bill of rights include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis".
People might be interested in knowing that the hon. member who sponsors this bill not only did not speak for
or against that private member's motion but in fact he could not make his way from the city of Ottawa to this Chamber to vote for it.
In addition, we have been told over and over that private members' business is non-partisan and should be non-partisan, that there should be a free vote. However, when we came into this House to vote on that private member's motion, the government Whip turned to his members. The government voted against a child protection commission and a children's bill of rights.
Again, I speak in favour of this bill. I am sure the hon. member and the member from Don Valley North both feel that what they are doing is going to help children. I hope they are right. But to have a child day without child policy and policy that will protect children is not going to solve the problems of children in this country.
Motion agreed to, bill read the third time and passed.
